title: Modeling directly from antibody levels
text: Proposed model Consider two-component Gaussian mixture model antibody level \(Z\), component \(Z_j\) represent antibody level arising 2 latent sub-populations \(j \\{, S\}\) (.e., Infected Susceptible groups). Let \(f_j(z_j|\theta_j)\) denotes density component \(Z_j\), \(\theta_I\) \(\theta_S\) parameters Susceptible Infected components respectively. \(\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()\) age-dependent mixing probability (.e., true prevalence), density mixture formulated \[ f(z|z_I, z_S,) = (1-\pi_{\text{TRUE}}())f_S(z_S|\theta_S)+\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()f_I(z_I|\theta_I) \] age-specific mean antibody level \(E(Z|)\) thus equals \[ \mu() = (1-\pi_{\text{TRUE}}())\mu_S+\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()\mu_I\] true prevalence can calculated \[ \pi_{\text{TRUE}}() = \frac{\mu() - \mu_S}{\mu_I - \mu_S} \] Force infection can inferred \[ \lambda_{TRUE} = \frac{\mu'()}{\mu_I - \mu()} \] Refer Chapter 11.3 book Hens et al. (2012) detailed explanation method. Fitting data General workflow: Step 1: Fit antibody level data 2-component mixture model Step 2: fitted mixture model, estimate seroprevalence FOI fit antibody data, use mixture_model function  sero-prevalence FOI can esimated using function estimate_from_mixture
code: df <- vzv_be_2001_2003[vzv_be_2001_2003$age < 40.5,] df <- df[order(df$age),] data <- df$VZVmIUml model <- mixture_model(antibody_level = data) model$info #>  #> Parameters: #>       pi    mu  sigma #> 1 0.1088 2.349 0.6804 #> 2 0.8912 6.439 0.9437 #>  #> Distribution: #> [1] "norm" #>  #> Constraints: #>    conpi    conmu consigma  #>   "NONE"   "NONE"   "NONE" plot(model) est_mixture <- estimate_from_mixture(df$age, data, mixture_model = model, threshold_status = df$seropositive, sp=83, monotonize = FALSE) plot(est_mixture) #> Warning: No shared levels found between `names(values)` of the manual scale and the #> data's fill values.

title: Nonparametric model
text: Proposed model Within local polynomial framework, linear predictor \(\eta()\) approximated locally one particular value \(a_0\) age line (local linear, degree \(p=1\)) parabola (local quadratic, degree \(p=2\)). general degree \(p\), linear predictor neighbor \(a_0\), labeled \(a_i\) Taylor approximation \[ \eta(a_i) = \eta(a_0) + \eta^{(1)}(a_0)(a_i - a_0) + \frac{\eta^{(2)}(a_0)}{2}(a_i - a_0)^2 + ... + \frac{\eta^{(p)}(a_0)}{p!}(a_i - a_0)^p \] estimator \(k\)-th derivative \(\eta(a_0)\), \(k = 0,1,…,p\) (degree local polynomial) followed: \[ \hat{\eta}^{(k)}(a_0) = k!\hat{\beta}_k(a_0) \] estimator prevalence age \(a_0\) given \[ \hat{\pi}(a_0) = g^{-1}\{ \hat{\beta}_0(a_0) \} \] \(g\) link function estimator force infection age \(a_0\) assuming \(p \ge 1\) followed \[ \hat{\lambda}(a_0) = \hat{\beta}_1(a_0) \delta \{ \hat{\beta}_0 (a_0) \} \] \(\delta \{ \hat{\beta}_0(a_0) \} = \frac{dg^{-1} \{ \hat{\beta}_0(a_0) \} } {d\hat{\beta}_0(a_0)}\) Refer Chapter 7.1 book Hens et al. (2012) detailed explanation method. Fitting data Use plot_gcv() show GCV curves nearest neighbor method (left) constant bandwidth (right).  Use lp_model() fit local estimation polynomials.
code: mump <- mumps_uk_1986_1987 plot_gcv(    mump$age, mump$pos, mump$tot,    nn_seq = seq(0.2, 0.8, by=0.1),    h_seq = seq(5, 25, by=1)  ) lp <- lp_model(mump, kern="tcub", nn=0.7, deg=2) plot(lp)

title: Parametric models
text: Proposed model Farrington’s model, force infection defined non-negative \(\lambda() \geq 0\) increases peak linear fashion followed exponential decrease \[ \lambda() = (\alpha - \gamma)e^{-\beta } + \gamma \] \(\gamma\) called long term residual FOI, \(\rightarrow \infty\) , \(\lambda () \rightarrow \gamma\) Integrating \(\lambda()\) results following non-linear model prevalence \[ \pi () = 1 - e^{-\int_0^\lambda(s) ds} \\ = 1 - exp\{ \frac{\alpha}{\beta}ae^{-\beta } + \frac{1}{\beta}(\frac{\alpha}{\beta} - \gamma)(e^{-\beta } - 1) -\gamma \} \] Fitting data Use farrington_model() fit Farrington’s model.
code: farrington_md <- farrington_model(    rubella_uk_1986_1987,    start=list(alpha=0.07,beta=0.1,gamma=0.03)    ) plot(farrington_md)

title: Model repeated cross-sectional data
text: monitor changes population’s seroprevalence time, modelers often conduct multiple cross-sectional surveys different time points, using new representative sample. resulting data known repeated cross-sectional data. Proposed approach model repeated cross-sectional serological data, serosv offers age_time_model() function implements following workflow: Fit age-specific seroprevalence survey period Monotonize age-specific birth-cohort-specific prevalence time Fit monotonized age-specific seroprevalence survey period Fitting data function expects input data following columns: Either age status (linelisting) age pos + tot (aggregated) column date survey (specified via time_col argument) column id survey period (specified via grouping_col argument) monotonization method can specified via monotonize_method argument, serosv currently supports 2 options: Pooled adjacent violators average (monotonize_method = "pava") Shape constrained additive model (monotonize_method = "scam") users can also configure monotonize either: Age-specific seroprevalence time (age_correct = FALSE) birth cohort specific seroprevalence time (age_correct=TRUE) output data.frame dimension [number survey, 9], row corresponds single survey period. columns : column id survey period df - input data.frame corresponding survey period info - model seroprevalence monotonized_info - model monotonized seroprevalence monotonized_ci_mod - model monotonized confidence interval sp - predicted seroprevalence given input data foi - estimated force infection sp monotonized_sp - predicted monotonized seroprevalence given input data monotonized_foi - estimated force infection monotonized_sp visualization, plot function age_time_model offers following configurations facet whether visualize result survey period separately (facet=TRUE) single plot (facet=FALSE) modtype choose model visualize, model fitted input data (modtype="non-monotonized") monotonized data (modtype="monotonized") Example: output model PAVA monotonization    Example: output model SCAM monotonization

title: Semiparametric model
text: Proposed model general model relating prevalence age can written GLM \[ g(P(Y_i = 1| _i)) = g(\pi(a_i)) = \eta(a_i) \] \(g\) link function \(\eta\) linear predictor linear predictor can estimated semi-parametrically using penalized spline truncated power basis functions degree \(p\) fixed knots \(\kappa_1,..., \kappa_k\) followed \[ \eta(a_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1a_i + ... + \beta_p a_i^p + \Sigma_{k=1}^ku_k(a_i - \kappa_k)^p_+ \] \[ (a_i - \kappa_k)^p_+ = \begin{cases} 0, & a_i \le \kappa_k \\ (a_i - \kappa_k)^p, & a_i > \kappa_k \end{cases} \] matrix notation, mean structure model \(\eta(a_i)\) becomes \[ \eta = \textbf{X}\beta + \textbf{Zu} \] \(\eta = [\eta(a_i) ... \eta(a_N) ]^T\), \(\beta = [\beta_0 \beta_1 .... \beta_p]^T\), \(\textbf{u} = [u_1 u_2 ... u_k]^T\) regression corresponding design matrices \[ \textbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a_1 & a_1^2 & ... & a_1^p \\ 1 & a_2 & a_2^2 & ... & a_2^p \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \dots & \vdots \\ 1 & a_N & a_N^2 & ... & a_N^p \end{bmatrix}, \textbf{Z} = \begin{bmatrix} (a_1 - \kappa_1 )_+^p & (a_1 - \kappa_2 )_+^p & \dots & (a_1 - \kappa_k)_+^p \\ (a_2 - \kappa_1 )_+^p & (a_2 - \kappa_2 )_+^p & \dots & (a_2 - \kappa_k)_+^p \\ \vdots & \vdots & \dots & \vdots \\ (a_N - \kappa_1 )_+^p & (a_N - \kappa_2 )_+^p & \dots & (a_N - \kappa_k)_+^p \end{bmatrix} \] FOI can derived \[ \hat{\lambda}(a_i) = [\hat{\beta_1} , 2\hat{\beta_2}a_i, ..., p \hat{\beta} a_i ^{p-1} + \Sigma^k_{k=1} p \hat{u}_k(a_i - \kappa_k)^{p-1}_+] \delta(\hat{\eta}(a_i)) \] \(\delta(.)\) determined link function used model

title: Semiparametric model
text: Proposed approach first approach fit model maximizing following penalized likelihood : \(X\beta + Zu\) predictor \(D\) known semi-definite penalty matrix (Wahba 1978), (Green Silverman 1993) \(y\) response vector \(\textbf{1}\) unit vector, \(c(.)\) determined link function used \(\lambda\) smoothing parameter (larger values –> smoother curves) \(\phi\) overdispersion parameter equals 1 overdispersion Refer Chapter 8.2.1 book Hens et al. (2012) detailed explanation method. Fitting data fit data using penalized likelihood framework, specify framework = "pl" Basis function can defined via s parameter, values s includes: "tp" thin plate regression splines "cr" cubic regression splines "ps" P-splines proposed (Eilers Marx 1996) "ad" Adaptive smoothers options, refer mgcv documentation (Wood 2017)
code: pl <- parvob19_be_2001_2003 %>%    rename(status = seropositive) %>%    penalized_spline_model(s = "tp", framework = "pl")  pl$info #>  #> Family: binomial  #> Link function: logit  #>  #> Formula: #> spos ~ s(age, bs = s, sp = sp) #>  #> Estimated degrees of freedom: #> 6.16  total = 7.16  #>  #> UBRE score: 0.1206458 plot(pl)

title: Semiparametric model
text: Proposed approach Looking back (1), constraint \(\textbf{u}\) \(\Sigma_ku_k^2 < C\) positive value \(C\) equivalent choosing \((\beta, \textbf{u})\) maximise (1) \(D = diag(\textbf{0}, \textbf{1})\) \(\textbf{0}\) denotes zero vector length \(p+1\) \(\textbf{1}\) denotes unit vector length \(K\) fixed value \(\lambda\) equivalent fitting following generalized linear mixed model Ngo Wand (2004) \[ f(y|u) = exp\{ \phi^{-1} [y^T(X\beta + Zu) - c(X\beta + Zu)] + 1^Tc(y)\},\\ u \sim N(0, G) \] similar notations \(G = \sigma^2_uI_{K \times K}\) Thus \(Z\) penalized assuming corresponding coefficients \(\textbf{u}\) random effect \(\textbf{u} \sim N(\textbf{0}, \mathbf{\sigma}^2_u \textbf{})\). Refer Chapter 8.2.2 book Hens et al. (2012) detailed explanation method. Fitting data fit data using penalized likelihood framework, specify framework = "glmm"
code: glmm <- parvob19_be_2001_2003 %>%    rename(status = seropositive) %>%    penalized_spline_model(s = "tp", framework = "glmm")  #>  #>  Maximum number of PQL iterations:  20 #> iteration 1 #> iteration 2 #> iteration 3 #> iteration 4 glmm$info$gam #>  #> Family: binomial  #> Link function: logit  #>  #> Formula: #> spos ~ s(age, bs = s, sp = sp) #>  #> Estimated degrees of freedom: #> 6.45  total = 7.45 plot(glmm)

title: SIR model
text:
Proposed model Let’s consider transmission model consists 3 compartments: susceptible (S), infected (), recovered (R) following assumptions: Individuals born susceptible group (exposure time age individual) transfer infected class recovered class Recovered individuals gained lifelong immunity Age homogeneity described system 3 differential equations \[  egin{cases}  rac{dS(t)}{dt} = B(t) (1-p) - \lambda(t)S(t) - \mu S(t) \  rac{dI(t)}{dt} = \lambda(t)S(t) - 
u (t) - \mu (t) - \alpha (t)  \  rac{dR(t)}{dt} =  B(t) p + 
u (t) - \mu R(t) \end{cases} \] : \(B(t) = \mu N(t)\) \(\lambda(t) =  eta (t)\) \( eta\) transmission rate \(\mu\) natural death rate \(
u\) recovery rate \(\alpha\) disease related death rate \(p\) proportion newborn vaccinated moved directly recovered compartment Simulating data simulate basic SIR model, use sir_basic_model() specify following parameters state - initial population compartment times - time sequence parameters - parameters SIR model
code: state <- c(S=4999, I=1, R=0) parameters <- c(   mu=1/75, # 1 divided by life expectancy (75 years old)   alpha=0, # no disease-related death   beta=0.0005, # transmission rate   nu=1, # 1 year for infected to recover   p=0 # no vaccination at birth ) times <- seq(0, 250, by=0.1) model <- sir_basic_model(times, state, parameters) model$parameters #>         mu      alpha       beta         nu          p  #> 0.01333333 0.00000000 0.00050000 1.00000000 0.00000000 plot(model)

Proposed model Let’s consider transmission model consists 3 compartments: susceptible (S), infected (), recovered (R) following assumptions: Time homogeneity Age heterogeneity Described system 3 differential equations \[  egin{cases}  rac{ds()}{da} = -\lambda s() \  rac{di()}{da} = \lambda s() - 
u ()  \  rac{dr()}{da} =  
u () \end{cases} \] : \(s(), (), r()\) proportion susceptible, infected, recovered population age group \(\) respectively \(\lambda\) force infection \(

title: SIR model
text: Proposed model Extends SIR model interacting sub-populations (different age groups) K subpopulations, WAIFW matrix mixing matrix given \[ C = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_{11} & \beta_{12}  & ... & \beta_{1K} \\ \beta_{21} & \beta_{22}  & ... & \beta_{2K} \\ \vdots & \vdots  & ... & \vdots \\ \beta_{K1} & \beta_{K2}  & ... & \beta_{KK} \\ \end{bmatrix} \] system differential equations \(th\) subpopulation given \[ \begin{cases} \frac{dS_i(t)}{dt} = -(\sum^K_{j=1}\beta_{ij}I_j(t)) S_i(t) + N_i\mu_i - \mu_i S_i(t) \\ \frac{dI_i(t)}{dt} = (\sum^K_{j=1}\beta_{ij}I_j(t)) S_i(t)  - (\nu_i + \mu_i) I_i(t)  \\ \frac{dR_i(t)}{dt} = \nu_i I_i(t)  - \mu_i R_i(t) \end{cases} \] Simulating data simulate SIR model subpopulations, use sir_subpops_model() specify following parameters state - initial proportion compartment population beta_matrix - WAIFW matrix, dimensions [K, K] times - time sequence parameters - parameters model
code: state <- c(   # proportion of each compartment for each population    s = c(0.8, 0.6),    i = c(0.2, 0.4),   r = c(  0,   0) ) beta_matrix <- matrix(   c(0.05, 0.00,     0.00, 0.05),   2 ) parameters <- list(   beta = beta_matrix,   nu = c(1/30, 1/30),   mu = 0.001 )  times<-seq(0,10000,by=0.5) model <- sir_subpops_model(times, state, parameters) model$parameters #> $beta #>      [,1] [,2] #> [1,] 0.05 0.00 #> [2,] 0.00 0.05 #>  #> $nu #> [1] 0.03333333 0.03333333 #>  #> $mu #> [1] 0.001 #>  #> $k #> [1] 2 plot(model) # returns plot for each population #> $subpop_1 #>  #> $subpop_2

text:
Proposed model Extends SIR model 2 additional compartments: maternal immunity (M) exposed period (E) described following system ordinary differential equation \[  egin{cases}  rac{dM()}{da} = -(\gamma + \mu())M() \  rac{dS()}{da} = \gamma M() - (\lambda() + \mu()) S() \  rac{dE()}{da} = \lambda() S()  - (\sigma + \mu()) E() \  rac{dI()}{da} = \sigma() E()  - (
u + \mu()) ()  \  rac{dR()}{da} = 
u ()  - \mu() R() \end{cases} \] \(M(0)\) = B, number births population \(\gamma\) rate antibody decaying \(\lambda()\) force infection age \(\) \(\mu()\) natural death rate age \(\) \(\sigma\) rate becoming infected exposed \(

title: Estimate seroprevalence and FOI from a fixed mixture model — estimate_from_mixture
text: Antibody level (denoted \(Z\)) modeled using 2-component Gaussian mixture model. component \(Z_j\) (\(j \\{, S\}\)) represents antibody level latent Infected Susceptible sub-populations, following density \(f_j(z_j|\theta_j)\) Let \(\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()\) denotes age-dependent mixing probability (.e., true prevalence), density mixture formulated $$f(z|z_I, z_S,) = (1-\pi_{\text{TRUE}}())f_S(z_S|\theta_S)+\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()f_I(z_I|\theta_I)$$ mean \(E(Z|)\) thus equals $$\mu() = (1-\pi_{\text{TRUE}}())\mu_S+\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()\mu_I$$ true prevalence can computed $$\pi_{\text{TRUE}}() = \frac{\mu() - \mu_S}{\mu_I - \mu_S}$$ FOI can inferred $$\lambda_{TRUE} = \frac{\mu'()}{\mu_I - \mu()}$$ Function [serosv::mixture_model()] fits antibody level data \(f_S(z_S|\theta_S)\) \(f_I(z_I|\theta_I)\) Function [serosv::estimate_mixture()] estimate age-specific antibody level \(\mu()\) infer estimation \(\pi_{\text{TRUE}}()\) \(\lambda_{TRUE}\) Refer section 11.3. book Hens et al. (2012) details.

text: Consider model prevalence parametric form \(\pi(a_i, \alpha)\) \(\alpha\) parameter vector Bayesian framework, can constraint parameter space prior distribution \(P(\alpha)\) achieve monotonicity posterior distribution \(P(\pi_1, \pi_2, ..., \pi_m|y,n)\) : - \(n = (n_1, n_2, ..., n_m)\) \(n_i\) sample size age \(a_i\) - \(y = (y_1, y_2, ..., y_m)\) \(y_i\) number infected individual \(n_i\) sampled subjects Farrington model 3 parameters, prevalence formulated follow $$ \pi () = 1 - exp\{ \frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2}ae^{-\alpha_2 } + \frac{1}{\alpha_2}(\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2} - \alpha_3)(e^{-\alpha_2 } - 1) -\alpha_3 \} $$ likelihood model defined \(y_i \sim Bin(n_i, \pi_i), \text{  } = 1,2,3,...m\) constraint parameter space can incorporated assuming  truncated normal distribution components \(\alpha\), \(\alpha = (\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3)\) \(\pi_i = \pi(a_i,\alpha)\) flat hyperpriors defined \(\mu_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10000)\) \(\tau^{-2}_j \sim \Gamma(100,100)\) Farrington model 2 parameters, equivalent previous model \(\alpha_3 = 0\) Log logistic model, seroprevalence instead defined $$\pi() = \frac{\beta ^\alpha}{1 + \beta ^\alpha}, \text{ } \alpha, \beta > 0$$ likelihood similarly defined \(y_i \sim Bin(n_i, \pi_i))\) prior model \(\alpha_1\) specified \(\alpha_1 \sim \text{truncated  } \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \tau_1)\) flat hyperpriors Farrington model \(\beta\) constrained positive specifying \(\alpha_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \tau_2)\) Refer section Chapter 10.3 book Hens et al. (2012) details.

title: Penalized Spline model — penalized_spline_model
text: semi-parametric model, predictor formulated penalized spline truncated power basis functions degree \(p\) fixed knots \(\kappa_1,..., \kappa_k\) followed $$ \eta(a_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1a_i + ... + \beta_p a_i^p + \Sigma_{k=1}^ku_k(a_i - \kappa_k)^p_+ $$ - : $$ (a_i - \kappa_k)^p_+ = \begin{cases} 0, & a_i \le \kappa_k \\ (a_i - \kappa_k)^p, & a_i > \kappa_k \end{cases} $$ FOI can derived $$\hat{\lambda}(a_i) = [\hat{\beta_1} , 2\hat{\beta_2}a_i, ..., p \hat{\beta} a_i ^{p-1} + \Sigma^k_{k=1} p \hat{u}_k(a_i - \kappa_k)^{p-1}_+] \delta(\hat{\eta}(a_i)) $$ \(\delta(.)\) determined link function used model matrix annotation, mean structure model \(\eta(a_i)\) becomes $$\eta = \textbf{X}\beta + \textbf{Zu}$$ \(\eta = [\eta(a_i) ... \eta(a_N) ]^T\), \(\beta = [\beta_0 \beta_1 .... \beta_p]^T\), \(\textbf{u} = [u_1 u_2 ... u_k]^T\) regression corresponding design matrices $$\textbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a_1 & a_1^2 & ... & a_1^p \\ 1 & a_2 & a_2^2 & ... & a_2^p \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \dots & \vdots \\ 1 & a_N & a_N^2 & ... & a_N^p \end{bmatrix}, \textbf{Z} = \begin{bmatrix} (a_1 - \kappa_1 )_+^p & (a_1 - \kappa_2 )_+^p & \dots & (a_1 - \kappa_k)_+^p \\ (a_2 - \kappa_1 )_+^p & (a_2 - \kappa_2 )_+^p & \dots & (a_2 - \kappa_k)_+^p \\ \vdots & \vdots & \dots & \vdots \\ (a_N - \kappa_1 )_+^p & (a_N - \kappa_2 )_+^p & \dots & (a_N - \kappa_k)_+^p \end{bmatrix} $$ penalized likelihood framework, model fitted maximizing following likelihood $$ \phi^{-1}[y^T(\textbf{X}\beta + \textbf{Zu} ) -  \textbf{1}^Tc(\textbf{X}\beta + \textbf{Zu} )] - \frac{1}{2}\lambda^2 \begin{bmatrix} \beta \\ \textbf{u} \end{bmatrix}^T D\begin{bmatrix} \beta \\ \textbf{u} \end{bmatrix} $$ : - \(X\beta + Zu\) predictor - \(D\) known semi-definite penalty matrix [@Wahba1978], [@Green1993] - \(y\) response vector - \(\textbf{1}\) unit vector, \(c(.)\) determined link function used - \(\lambda\) smoothing parameter (larger values –> smoother curves) - \(\phi\) overdispersion parameter equals 1 overdispersion mixed model framework, model instead treats coefficients \(\textbf{u}\) likelihood formulation random effects \(\textbf{u} \sim N(\textbf{0}, \mathbf{\sigma}^2_u \textbf{})\) Refer section 8.1 8.2 book Hens et al. (2012) details.

title: SIR Model with Interacting Subpopulations — sir_subpops_model
text: Follow SIR model sub populations described book Hens et al. (section 3.5.1.) K subpopulations, WAIFW matrix mixing matrix given $$ C = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_{11} & \beta_{12}  & ... & \beta_{1K} \\ \beta_{21} & \beta_{22}  & ... & \beta_{2K} \\ \vdots & \vdots  & ... & \vdots \\ \beta_{K1} & \beta_{K2}  & ... & \beta_{KK} \\ \end{bmatrix} $$ \(^{th}\) sub population described following system differential equations $$ \begin{cases} \frac{dS_i(t)}{dt} = -(\sum^K_{j=1}\beta_{ij}I_j(t)) S_i(t) + N_i\mu_i - \mu_i S_i(t) \\ \frac{dI_i(t)}{dt} = (\sum^K_{j=1}\beta_{ij}I_j(t)) S_i(t)  - (\nu_i + \mu_i) I_i(t)  \\ \frac{dR_i(t)}{dt} = \nu_i I_i(t)  - \mu_i R_i(t) \end{cases} $$
